Original Video Credit: IG/robotstory.ae Packed tightly inside its transport case, the humanoid robot begins unfolding its articulated limbs before extending both feet onto the floor. It then raises its torso, positions itself on the edge of the case, and transitions into a full standing posture without being physically lifted by a person. Coordinated electric joints and onboard control systems manage the sequence by continuously controlling limb positions and balance as the robot shifts its weight. Its arms and legs work together to create stable points of support while the body moves from a folded position to standing. Self-deployment demonstrates how humanoid robots can perform more than programmed walking or manipulation tasks. Being able to transition between complex body positions with minimal human assistance could make these machines easier to transport, deploy, and operate in real-world environments. Robot plays "The Butterfly Lovers" on the erhu | 二胡 | 梁祝 | 乐器 The Erhu is a traditional Chinese bowed string instrument. It originated in the Tang Dynasty, with its predecessor being the "Xiqin" played by northern ethnic minorities. Although its structure is simple — a wooden sound box covered with python skin at the front, a neck standing upright on it, and two strings sounded by a bow — it possesses great acoustic wisdom. The timbre of the Erhu closely resembles the human voice, capable of vividly expressing emotions such as joy, anger, sorrow, and happiness.#robot #robotics #erhu #music #future

I spent days teaching a 3D-printed robot duck to walk. Most of that time, it was falling over. It’s my own build of the Open Duck Mini. The open-source, BDX-inspired biped created by Antoine Pirrone. The whole thing is 3D-printed and runs on hobby-grade servos instead of industrial actuators, which is what makes it buildable on a normal budget and also what makes it so hard to get walking. The hard part wasn’t the printing or the assembly. It was the sim-to-real gap. A gait that walks perfectly in MuJoCo hits real-world joint slop, servo lag, and a center of mass that won’t sit still, and just before you know it, the duck face plants into the floor. It took me 40+ calibration passes before it could take three steps without tipping! What the build came down to: • 3D-printed chassis • Per-joint offset calibration (where most of the pain lived) • Policy training in simulation (MuJoCo / Isaac Lab) • Build guide + docs via Tnkr • A lot of failed walks Real hardware. Real failures. Real progress.

A humanoid robot named Joko Prabuwesi went viral after a video showed it unleashing a series of fast Shaolin-style martial arts kicks at office workers inside a corporate headquarters over the weekend. The robot lunged at staff as they struggled to hold it back while it carried out the choreographed combat moves. At first, many people thought the footage was AI-generated or a digital animation because of how realistic it looked. Later, independent technical verification confirmed the video was real and showed an actual robot moving inside a real workplace. Although the robot's smooth movements, balance and joint control were genuine, it wasn't acting on its own or experiencing a malfunction. Handlers from an Indonesian digital media company said the scene was a pre-programmed marketing demonstration to show off the robot's motor control. The kung fu routine had been loaded into its memory before the event.

Industrial humanoid robots are looking less humanlike every day.  The Chinese company LimX Dynamics just shared footage of its TRON 2 dual-arm robot integrated with an industrial robotic arm. The TRON 2 multi-form-factor robot has gone viral in the past for its modular design that can transform into a humanoid, a quadruped, or even be combined into a centaur.    In the industrial setup, TRON 2 is mounted onto a traditional robotic arm to extend its reach. It uses a custom attachment to hold and operate a power drill and nailer to assemble wooden frames and panels. It then applies spray finishing.    The TRON 2 is priced starting around $7,000 in China but international pricing begins around $13,000.   Shenzhen-based LimX is scaling production of its TRON platform, along with its full-sized humanoid robot Oli, and its sister, Luna, after securing around $400 million so far in 2026. Valued at $2.2 billion, it's one of many Chinese robotics startups racing toward a public listing. #robotics #robot #industrialrobot #ai #automation

I'm sorry... but who looked at this and said, "Yep, that's the design!"? 🤣 If your rescue robot walks out of the woods looking like a seven-foot-tall mechanical demon carrying a chainsaw... maybe the branding department got a little carried away. 😂 They could have made it look like a normal industrial robot. Instead they named the company after a satyress (a mythical goat-like creature), gave it giant ram's horns, painted it matte black, and then acted surprised when the internet said, "What in the horror movie is THAT?" 😆 Sure, the company says the shape protects sensors and helps it work in dangerous environments. But let's be honest... the dramatic mythological look is also part of the branding. It gets people talking—and judging by all of us arguing about it, it worked. 😄 If I ever need rescuing in the woods and this thing comes walking toward me with glowing eyes... my first thought isn't going to be, "Thank goodness!" It's going to be, "Well... this is one interesting way to meet my maker." 🤣👹🤖

Hugging Face is ramping up production of its new open-source robotic ducks after the first 24 hours of preorders blew past what it can ship by year's end.    The Brooklyn-based company launched its $399 Microduck in four colorways shortly after news broke that NVIDIA was buying the AI firm for around $12.9 billion. Hugging Face developed the AI-powered robot in collaboration with Pollen Robotics, its French subsidiary that also made the research-grade humanoid robot, Reachy, and its desktop version for consumers, the Reachy Mini.    The Miniduck is a 25 cm (10 inch) bipedal robot that weighs under 800 grams (1.8 lbs). It has 15 motors in its legs, neck, and head, a beak that can pick up small objects. It moves faster with optional wheels.    The robot perceives its surroundings with a front camera and a small LiDAR depth sensor. A Chinese Rockchip processor powers the duck's onboard artificial intelligence. According to Hugging Face, the Microduck can do basic moves out the box, while users can teach it new tricks in simulation.   Hugging Face says it sold more than $2.5 million of Microducks in the first day of preorders, which equates to more than 6,500 units. #robot #robotics #microduck #robotduck #huggingface
